stories.headline: TRUMP REINSTATES HORMUZ BLOCKADE, IMPOSES 20% TRANSIT FEE AS OIL ROCKETS AND STOCKS SELL OFF
stories.body: Trump announced the U.S. would reimpose a blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and charge a 20% fee on all cargo shipped through the waterway after the U.S. and Iran traded fresh strikes over the weekend, including hits on energy infrastructure. The news erased hopes of a mid-June de-escalation and sent WTI up 9.4% to $78.14 and Brent up 9.6% to $83.80, while the S&P 500 fell 0.79% to 7,515.34.
stories.explain: A 'blockade' shifts the oil market's calculation from a probability-weighted risk premium to something closer to a confirmed supply disruption, which is why crude's reaction (+9%+) dwarfed the equity market's (-0.79%) — oil prices the physical chokepoint directly, while stocks discount it through earnings and multiple effects that take longer to work through. The 20% transit fee functions like a tax on roughly a fifth of global seaborne oil trade, meaning it can add to input costs and headline inflation even without a single barrel failing to reach a buyer.

stories.headline: BRENT LOGS BIGGEST ONE-DAY GAIN SINCE 2020, WTI SETTLES AT $78.14 ON HORMUZ BLOCKADE
stories.body: Brent crude jumped 9.6% to settle at $83.80 a barrel — its highest close in about a month and its largest one-day percentage gain in more than six years — while WTI rose 9.4% to settle at $78.14. Semiconductor names bore collateral damage: the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index sank as SK Hynix fell 6.1% and Sandisk, Marvell, and Western Digital dropped between 6.5% and 12.3%, extending a global chip selloff.
stories.explain: Oil's one-day jump is a 'gap' move — the market had spent two weeks pricing OUT the war premium on diplomatic optimism, so when the blockade was reinstated, the adjustment happened in a single session rather than gradually, which is what produces a move of this size. Semiconductor stocks selling off alongside an oil-driven equity selloff shows how energy shocks propagate into growth-sensitive sectors first: chipmakers carry high fixed costs and long capex cycles, making their valuations unusually sensitive to any rise in the discount rate or slowdown in global growth expectations.

stories.headline: S&P 500 SLIDES 0.79%, NASDAQ TUMBLES ON CHIP-SECTOR ROUT AS TRADERS BRACE FOR CPI
stories.body: The S&P 500 fell 0.79% to 7,515.34 and the Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.55% to 25,873.18 (the Nasdaq-100 fell roughly 1.7%) as the reignited Iran conflict and a broadening semiconductor selloff overshadowed the coming start of bank earnings season. The Dow held up better, down just 0.26% to 52,498.64, underscoring how concentrated Monday's damage was in tech.
stories.explain: The gap between the Dow's 0.26% decline and the Nasdaq's roughly 1.6-1.7% drop is a concentration story: the Dow's price-weighted, industrial-heavy composition insulated it from a selloff concentrated almost entirely in semiconductors and AI-adjacent names, the same stocks that drove most of the index's 2025-26 gains. That divergence is worth tracking into Tuesday's CPI — if the data confirms the Fed's hawkish tilt, the stocks most exposed to higher discount rates are structurally first to reprice.

stories.headline: TREASURY YIELDS HIT 16-MONTH HIGHS AS OIL SHOCK COLLIDES WITH A FED ALREADY DEBATING A HIKE
stories.body: The 2-year Treasury yield rose as much as 4 bps to 4.25% Monday — its highest since February 2025 — and the 10-year climbed to 4.58% (+3 bps) as the weekend's oil shock reinforced bets that the Fed could raise rates before September; futures markets are pricing roughly a 70% probability of a hike, a sharp reversal from the cut expectations that dominated a year ago. Tuesday's June CPI report (core seen +0.2% m/m, +2.8% y/y) now carries extra weight ahead of Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first congressional testimony Tuesday and Wednesday.
stories.explain: The 2-year yield is the market's cleanest proxy for the expected path of Fed policy over the next two years, since it's short enough to be dominated by rate expectations rather than the term premium and long-run growth assumptions baked into the 10-year — that's why it, not the 10-year, hit a fresh cycle high Monday. An oil-driven spike in headline CPI doesn't directly change the Fed's preferred core-inflation target, but it raises the risk that inflation expectations de-anchor, which is precisely the channel a hawkish Fed under Warsh would cite to justify a hike even though a rate increase does nothing to add oil supply.

stories.headline: GOLD FALLS DESPITE WAR RISK AS RISING REAL YIELDS OVERPOWER SAFE-HAVEN DEMAND
stories.body: Gold fell more than 2% to around $4,020 an ounce Monday — a second straight day of losses — even as the Iran conflict escalated, a counterintuitive move that reflects surging Treasury yields and expectations that the Fed's next move could be a hike rather than a cut. The dollar index was essentially flat at 100.93 (-0.02%), meaning gold's drop wasn't a currency story — it was a real-yields story.
stories.explain: Gold pays no yield, so its opportunity cost rises directly with real interest rates; when 2-year Treasury yields jump to a 16-month high on hike expectations, holding gold becomes more expensive relative to holding short-term Treasurys, even if the same headlines are geopolitically bullish for the metal. This is the mechanism that separates gold's 'safe-haven' reputation from its actual price behavior: gold tends to rally on crises the Fed is expected to answer with rate cuts, and struggles on crises — like an oil supply shock — that push the Fed toward tightening instead.

stories.headline: KANSAS LANDS NATION'S NO. 1 RECRUIT AS OFFSEASON ROSTER OVERHAUL ACCELERATES ACROSS COLLEGE HOOPS
stories.body: Kansas secured a commitment from the nation's top-ranked incoming prospect, while Kentucky added Iowa State transfer forward Milan Momcilovic — this spring's top transfer-portal target — and North Carolina replaced departed center Henri Veesaar with two international signees. More than 2,700 players have moved through the transfer portal since Michigan beat UConn for the national title, an offseason churn rate reshaping preseason rankings before October practice opens.

stories.headline: AJ DYBANTSA HEADLINES SUMMER LEAGUE AS LEBRON JAMES EXPLORES A LANDING SPOT AFTER LEAVING THE LAKERS
stories.body: No. 1 pick AJ Dybantsa is averaging 25 points per game and has his Summer League team to 2-0 in Las Vegas, while No. 2 pick Darryn Peterson has scored 23-plus points in each of his four summer outings. Off the court, LeBron James has informed the Lakers he won't return in 2026-27, with his camp reportedly eyeing the Knicks, 76ers, and Celtics as potential destinations.

stories.headline: SEAHAWKS' RECORD $9.6B SALE HEADLINES A QUIET NFL MONDAY FOCUSED ON TRAINING-CAMP PREP
stories.body: The Paul Allen Estate's agreement to sell the Seahawks to a Khosla family-led group for $9.612 billion — an NFL record, roughly 50% above the prior high — continued to dominate league business news, with the deal still needing ratification from at least 24 of the other 31 owners. Elsewhere, the Packers extended linebacker Isaiah McDuffie and teams around the league finalized rookie contracts ahead of training camps opening later this month.

stories.headline: TRANSFER PORTAL QB MARKET SHIFTS AS $10M MIAMI MOVE AND OKLAHOMA'S JASON WITTEN HIRE RESHAPE ROSTERS
stories.body: Duke transfer quarterback Darian Mensah's reported $10 million move to Miami continues to reverberate through ACC title odds, while Oklahoma rebuilt its tight end room with three transfers and hired former NFL tight end Jason Witten as position coach. With the 2026 cycle's portal window having closed back in January, rosters are locked in for fall camp, leaving late-summer buzz focused on NIL valuations — including a reported $4 million deal for the top transfer-portal offensive lineman.

sports.detail: Enter the All-Star break at 48-49 after beating Tampa Bay 8-2 Sunday behind a Randy Arozarena three-run homer. The All-Star Game is Tuesday (8 PM ET, Citizens Bank Park); Seattle returns Friday to open a series vs. the Giants at T-Mobile Park.
Fell to the Knicks 86-75 in Summer League Monday despite 24 points from Chaz Lanier (8-for-13, 3-for-3 from three). Next: Wednesday 7/15, 6 PM ET vs. Suns (ESPNU).

The Paul Allen Estate's agreement to sell the franchise to a Khosla family-led group for a record $9.612B still needs ratification from at least 24 of the other 31 owners. Training camp opens July 25 in Renton; Football Fest is Aug. 8 at Lumen Field.

Landed a 4-star cornerback commitment, the class's highest-rated pledge, while still chasing a second corner and offensive line help. RB Jordan Washington is targeting a late-July return from his spring injury ahead of fall camp.

Added commitments from Croatian forward Boris Tišma and Australian guard Tristan Devers, plus new assistant coach DeAndre Haynes (ex-Marquette). F Hannes Steinbach (14th overall to Charlotte) remains the program's top NBA export as Danny Sprinkle rebuilds after losing Zoom Diallo to the portal.

deepDive.title: The Fed Is Debating a Hike, Not a Cut — Why That Makes Today's Oil Shock Hit Harder
content: Monday's tape only makes sense once you drop the assumption that the Fed's next move is a cut. The 2-year Treasury yield jumped as much as 4 bps to 4.25%, its highest since February 2025, right as WTI spiked 9.4% to $78.14 on a reinstated Strait of Hormuz blockade. Futures markets are now pricing roughly a 70% probability of a Fed rate hike before September — a full reversal from the cut-cycle narrative that dominated a year ago. That backdrop is why Tuesday's CPI print and Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first congressional testimony (House on the 14th, Senate on the 15th) matter more than they would in a normal easing cycle.

The mechanism runs through which yield moves and why. The 2-year is the market's cleanest read on the expected policy path over the Fed's actual decision horizon, since it carries little term premium and almost no long-run growth speculation — both of which dilute the signal in the 10-year. When 2-year yields hit a cycle high on the same day oil spikes, it means traders think the Fed will treat this as inflationary fuel for a hike, not a demand shock that a cut could offset. Nine of 18 FOMC officials already projected at least one 2026 hike in their dot-plot submissions, and the committee revised its year-end inflation forecast up to 3.6%.

What most people miss is that a hike doesn't actually fix an oil-driven inflation problem — raising rates doesn't add a single barrel of crude to the market. The Fed's real target is the expectations channel: if households and firms start assuming higher gas prices will persist and get baked into wage and pricing decisions, that's when a supply shock becomes a demand-side inflation problem the Fed can address. This is the same logic that split the FOMC during 1970s oil shocks, when policymakers debated whether tightening into an energy-driven CPI spike would just add a recession on top of a supply problem without curing the inflation.

That's the lens for reading Tuesday and Wednesday. A hot core CPI print combined with a hawkish Warsh testimony would validate the 70% hike odds already priced in, likely pushing 2-year yields higher still, which is exactly the channel that hit gold Monday — real yields up, opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset up, price down, even amid a live war. A softer core print or a more cautious Warsh would do the opposite, and the assets most levered to that surprise — long-duration tech, gold, and the front end of the curve — are the ones to watch first.
